messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 71
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Painter
  trauma_type: Terrorism
  pcl5: 48

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Reassurance Seeking: I keep asking others to reassure me that I am okay, Emotion Control: I try hard to control my emotions, Avoid Going Out: Going out
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
  Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Can't Rely on Others: I can't rely on other people, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Sione Kaleo is a 71-year-old man of Pacific Islander background who has supported himself for decades as a house painter, taking pride in steady hands, careful lines, and the habit of working alone. He had been on a downtown commercial job last year when a bomb detonated outside a nearby office building. He remembers the blast with painful clarity: the crack of sound, the glass breaking outward, the force that threw him down against a wall and folded his body awkwardly onto one shoulder with his knees tucked under him as he tried to shield his head. Dust filled his mouth. There were sirens, people shouting, and the smell of smoke and hot metal. Even now, when the memory comes, it does not feel distant or story-like. It arrives sharply and against his will, with the scene intact in vivid detail, and his body seems to return to that exact position on the ground before he is fully aware of where he is.

In the weeks after the bombing, Sione found that the memory intruded at odd moments, especially when he heard a sudden bang from construction, a truck backfiring, or even a paint can dropped on concrete at work. What frightened him was not only remembering but how completely it took him over. He had come to believe that if his own mind and body could turn on him so suddenly, he could not rely on himself anymore. He no longer trusted his reactions, his judgment, or his ability to stay steady under pressure. The attack also altered how he saw everyone around him. The randomness of the bombing made him certain the world was dangerous in a basic, permanent way, and because no one had seen it coming, he felt other people could not really keep him safe either. The forceful, vivid quality of the memory seemed to prove this to him over and over: danger was close, and neither he nor anyone else could be counted on when it mattered.

From there, he began trying to manage himself tightly. Sione started putting great effort into controlling his emotions, especially in front of other people. If he felt panic rising, he would clamp down, hold his face still, and tell himself not to show anything. He also began asking for reassurance in a way that embarrassed him. He would call his sister after a loud noise and ask whether he sounded all right, whether she thought he was “losing it,” whether what he was feeling meant something was seriously wrong. He cut back more and more on going out unless he absolutely had to. Jobs that once would have been routine became difficult if they were in busy commercial areas, and he increasingly chose indoor residential work or postponed errands so he could stay close to home. These habits made sense to him because he was sure the world was unsafe and that he could not trust either his own coping or other people’s protection.

Over the following months, those ways of coping narrowed his life and seemed to make the problem larger. When he forced his feelings down, he became more preoccupied with whether he was managing them properly, and ordinary bodily shifts—a jump in his chest, tension in his shoulders—caught his attention quickly. When he stayed home, leaving the apartment felt even more exposed the next time. At work, being on a ladder with traffic below or hearing scaffolding clatter nearby could bring the bombing back into his mind with brutal immediacy, his body bracing into that same collapsed posture before he could stop it. After these moments he would seek reassurance again, asking family or a coworker if he was okay, if he had seemed strange, if they thought he could still handle working. The more he depended on others to calm him, the less confidence he had in his own ability to get through the next episode, and each retreat confirmed his sense that danger was everywhere and that he was no longer dependable to himself.

Being single, he has spent long stretches alone with these experiences. He still paints, but more irregularly, turning down certain jobs and avoiding crowded streets where sudden noise feels unbearable. He describes himself as an old man who should be tougher than this, yet he is increasingly convinced that one more surprise could undo him. What finally brought him to seek help was a recent incident on a job when a compressor kicked on unexpectedly and he dropped to the floor, curled protectively on his side, while a younger worker stared. Sione was shaken less by the noise itself than by the certainty that he had no control over what happened in his own mind and body. He wants relief from the memories that force their way in, but most of all he wants to know whether he can trust himself enough to go out, work, and live in the world again.
